source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer, Jones (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact (Science 342:468; preprint)
finding: Founding measure. For every pair of references in a paper, record the journal pair. Compare how often the pair is co-cited with how often a degree-preserving random citation network would produce it. The result is a z-score per journal pair. Negative z means atypical, positive means conventional.
numbers: 17.9 million WoS papers, 15,613 journals, over 122 million possible journal pairs. Summary stats per paper: median z (central tendency) and 10th percentile z (left tail).
limits: Unit is the journal pair, so novelty is only as fine as journal labels. Needs a full citation database. Only references inside WoS count (books excluded).
agent_relevance: Novelty here is a property of what is combined, scored against a null model of chance. A selector can use the same idea: rarity relative to what chance would give, not raw rarity.

source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer, Jones (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact (Science 342:468; preprint)
finding: Science is mostly conventional. Papers with a median z below zero are rare. Even the left tail is rarely atypical.
numbers: Median z below zero: 3.54% of papers in the 1980s, 2.67% in the 1990s. Half of papers have median z above 69.0 (1980s) and 99.5 (1990s). 10th percentile z below zero: 40.8% (1980s) and 40.7% (1990s).
limits: Descriptive for WoS 1980s-1990s only. Journal-pair z-scores grow with database size, so absolute values are not comparable across eras.
agent_relevance: Default output of any generator will be conventional. Atypical pairs are the exception even in human work, so a selector must look for them on purpose.

source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer, Jones (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact (Science 342:468; preprint)
finding: Core result: the best papers are very conventional with a small injection of atypical pairs. Hit rate is highest when median conventionality is high AND the left tail is atypical.
numbers: Hit = top 5% of citations in 8 years. Hit rate per 100 papers: high median + atypical tail 9.11 (about 2x the 5 baseline); high median, no atypical tail 5.82; low median + atypical tail 5.33; low on both 2.05.
quote: Papers with an intrusion of novelty into an otherwise exceptionally familiar mass of prior work are unusually likely to have high impact.
limits: Citation count is the only outcome. Hit rate is a binary 2x2 cut. Later work (Lin et al., Bornmann et al.) shows the measure and the outcome can diverge. Correlational, not causal.
agent_relevance: Supports a 'mostly familiar, one surprising link' rule for what the agent proposes in open mode. It is not 'maximise surprise'.

source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer, Jones (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact (Science 342:468; preprint)
finding: Peak impact sits at a very high level of conventionality, and an atypical tail adds impact at every level. Pattern held in all time periods, hit definitions and 243 fields.
numbers: Regression in 11 equal bins of median conventionality, field fixed effects. Peak impact at the 85th-95th percentile of median conventionality. Larger teams had higher impact at nearly every mix.
limits: Fixed effects only; author prestige, topic fashion and journal prestige not fully controlled in the main text.
agent_relevance: Suggests the optimum is near the conventional end, not mid-range. A selector that targets 'medium novelty' would miss it.

source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer, Jones (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact (Science 342:468; preprint)
finding: Teams insert atypical pairs more often than solo authors, without losing conventionality.
numbers: High tail novelty in 36.1% (1 author), 39.8% (2), 49.7% (3+) of papers: +37.7% for 3+ vs solo. KS tests on 10th-percentile z: solo vs pair p=0.016, pair vs team p=0.001, team vs solo p<0.001. Median z not different (p=0.768, 0.417, 0.164).
limits: Team size is a rough proxy for diverse knowledge; authors can differ in field mix. No control for self-selection into teams.
agent_relevance: Several independent agents or roles may raise tail novelty without lowering the conventional base. Weak analogy; the agents here are not independent (see G4).

source: Uzzi et al. (2013) Supplementary Online Material
finding: The null model: a Markov-chain Monte Carlo switching algorithm rewires citation links among all 17.9 million papers (302 million edges). It keeps each paper's number of references, its citations received, and the timing of those citations. 10 random copies of WoS, z computed against their mean and standard deviation.
numbers: Worked example: JACS-Life Sciences observed 469 co-citations vs null mean 3,147 (novel). Tetrahedron-Experientia observed 454 vs null mean 256 (conventional). Same raw count, opposite verdict. 1980 example: Tetrahedron-Experientia z=21.55, Tetrahedron-Life Sciences z=-17.67.
limits: Only 10 random networks, so the null standard deviation is estimated from 10 draws. Expensive to compute. Journal level only; the SOM notes text-based or topic-level versions as future options.
agent_relevance: Shows why raw rarity is a bad novelty score: popular sources co-occur by chance. Any LLM-based rarity score needs a base-rate correction too.

source: Uzzi et al. (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact (main text validation)
finding: Validation of the z-score is thin: same-discipline journal pairs have higher z than cross-discipline pairs, but cross-discipline pairs are not reliably novel.
numbers: Only 40.1% of interdisciplinary journal pairs had z below zero in the 1990s.
limits: Face validity only. The original paper has no check against expert judgement of novelty. That came later (Bornmann et al. 2019).
agent_relevance: Interdisciplinary does not equal novel. Distance between fields is not the same as surprise.

source: Bornmann, Tekles, Zhang, Ye (2019) Do we measure novelty when we analyze unusual combinations of cited references? Validation study on F1000Prime (J. Informetrics)
finding: First quantitative convergent-validity test of the Uzzi-type score (score U, with the Lee et al. 2015 revision) against expert judgement. U partly tracks expert 'novelty' tags. The Wang et al. 2017 score (W) mostly does not.
numbers: 23,206 biomedical papers (2013-2015) with F1000Prime faculty tags; Poisson regressions. One SD up in U: +7.47% 'new finding' tags (p<0.001, pseudo R2 0.33%), +17.71% 'hypothesis' tags, +28.78% 'technical advance', +58.78% 'novel drug target'.
limits: Effects are small (pseudo R2 under 3% in the models shown). Biomedicine only. F1000 tags come from selected, mostly positive recommendations. Pseudo R2 shows U explains little of the variation.
agent_relevance: Even the best-validated citation-based novelty score is a weak proxy for what experts call new. Do not use it as the only selector.

source: Bornmann, Tekles, Zhang, Ye (2019) Do we measure novelty when we analyze unusual combinations of cited references? Validation study on F1000Prime (J. Informetrics)
finding: Score U moves the wrong way for confirmation-type tags, as expected. A simple keyword-newness score (K, share of new keywords) was also computed for comparison and was not a clear winner.
numbers: U: 'confirmation' tag -13.45% per SD, 'good for teaching' -10.35%, 'refutation' -19.86% (all p<0.001). K was available for 23,041 papers; its coefficients are not tabulated here.
limits: Direction of 'controversial' and 'negative results' tags was not predicted well. Keyword score K is crude.
agent_relevance: Conventional work is correctly marked as conventional, which is the half of the job a rarity-based selector can do reliably.

source: Bornmann, Tekles, Zhang, Ye (2019) Do we measure novelty when we analyze unusual combinations of cited references? Validation study on F1000Prime (J. Informetrics)
finding: Qualitative caution cited: authors of landmark papers said their ideas were not necessarily inspired by their references. Cited references may not be where novelty comes from.
numbers: Tahamtan and Bornmann (2018) interviews, cited in the paper's intro; the quantitative study exists to test this worry.
limits: Second-hand here: the interview study itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: Novelty may sit in the idea, not in the citation list. For an LLM, the 'reference list' is the prompt context, so the proxy is even weaker.

source: Wang, Veugelers, Stephan (2017) Bibliometric measure of novelty (Research Policy 46:1416), via Bornmann et al. 2019 and Lin et al. 2021
finding: Alternative measure: count only NEW journal pairs (not co-cited before the focal paper, then co-cited at least once in the following 3 years), weighted by 1 minus cosine similarity of the two journals' co-citation profiles.
numbers: As reported by Bornmann et al.: novel papers get fewer citations early but more after several years, and are more likely to be big hits and to spawn follow-on hits.
limits: Not opened. Described only through Bornmann et al. (2019). Their own validation found W did not reproduce expert 'new finding' tags.
agent_relevance: Novelty pays late. A one-shot scorer that rewards immediate acceptance will undervalue it.

source: Lee, Walsh, Wang (2015) Creativity in scientific teams: Unpacking novelty and impact (Research Policy 44:684), via Bornmann et al. 2019
finding: Revised the Uzzi z-score into a per-paper novelty score and used it to separate novelty from impact in teams.
numbers: Not extracted: figures not read this session.
limits: Not opened. Cited as source of the revised 'score U' that Bornmann et al. validated.
agent_relevance: Another case where the measure is reused beyond its original use.

source: Foster, Rzhetsky, Evans (2015) Tradition and innovation in scientists' research strategies (ASR), via Lin et al. 2021
finding: Chemistry-based novelty: new combinations of chemical entities, and a tension between tradition and innovation. Cited as a parallel finding to Uzzi.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Not opened; second-hand only.
agent_relevance: Independent measure in a different data type (chemicals, not journals) giving a similar story.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2021) New directions in science emerge from disconnection and discord (arXiv 2103.03398)
finding: Extends Uzzi: highly atypical papers are about 2x more likely to be disruptive, even though the 'mixed' profile has the best hit rate.
numbers: Microsoft Academic Graph, 87.9 million articles, 1.04 billion citations. Highly atypical (10th pct z and median z both negative) papers: 61% vs 36% chance of being in a disruptive class vs conventional ones. Only 2.3% of papers are highly atypical, down from 3.9% (1970) to 1.4% (2000). Correlation typicality vs D-score -0.05 (p<0.001).
limits: Correlations are tiny (r=-0.05). The 61% vs 36% is a top-vs-bottom group comparison. Uses journal-pair z, so the same limits as Uzzi.
agent_relevance: Which measure you pick (hit rate vs disruption) changes whether 'mixed' or 'bold' wins. State the target before building the selector.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2021) New directions in science emerge from disconnection and discord (arXiv 2103.03398)
finding: Atypical work pays off late. Their citations grow after 10 years; conventional papers' citations flatten.
numbers: Sleeping Beauty Index vs atypicality r=0.08 (log-log, p<0.001). Cohorts 1970 (87,475 papers), 1980 (176,826), 1990 (318,914), 2000 (591,653); top 10% vs bottom 10% of median z. DNA double helix: D-score rose from 0.2 (1953) to about 0.8 after 10 years and 0.96 by 2018; Baltimore RNA paper D=-0.47.
limits: Two case studies are hand-picked. Delays of 10+ years mean recent novelty cannot be validated yet.
agent_relevance: Any evaluation of novelty from outputs measured within one session misses the delayed payoff. The agent cannot wait ten years, so it needs a proxy it knows is partial.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2021) New directions in science emerge from disconnection and discord (arXiv 2103.03398)
finding: First computational reformulation: atypicality as distance in a learned embedding space. Word2vec skip-gram on journal co-citation, whose inner product approximates pointwise mutual information (a revised z-score).
numbers: Embedding dimension 50, negative sampling 5, window 10. 1970 space: 2,429 journals; 2000 space: 8,009. Correlation of z-score with embedding inner product: Pearson 0.74 (p<0.001).
limits: Journal level and co-citation only. Correlation 0.74 leaves a lot unexplained. Not tested on text.
agent_relevance: Direct bridge to LLM-era novelty: z-score is a negative PMI, so embedding distance is a cheap stand-in. Same logic can be applied to a model's own embedding of concept pairs.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2021) New directions in science emerge from disconnection and discord (arXiv 2103.03398)
finding: Space of what counts as novel moves. Pairs that were atypical in 1970 (social science with computer science) were far less so by 2000.
numbers: Observed in t-SNE of 1970 vs 2000 journal embeddings. Qualitative, no single number.
limits: Qualitative, from figures.
agent_relevance: Novelty is relative to a reference corpus and date. An LLM's reference corpus is frozen at its training cutoff, so 'novel to the model' is not 'novel now'.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2021), introduction: survey of rival novelty measures
finding: Lists the rival ways to measure novelty: keyword combinations, chemical or biological entities (Foster 2015), patent classes (Youn 2015), knowledge-space distance (Shi 2019, Gebhart 2020), concept pairs (Hofstra 2020), and journal-pair z (Uzzi 2013).
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Literature list only.
agent_relevance: Shows the field already moved from journal pairs toward text and embeddings: the same step an LLM can take.

source: Krenn and Zeilinger (2020) Predicting research trends with semantic and neural networks (SemNet, arXiv 1906.06843)
finding: Concept co-occurrence network from 750,000 quantum-physics papers since 1919. A neural network trained on past network states predicts which unconnected concept pairs will become connected within 5 years. This is atypical-combination logic turned into a forecast.
numbers: ROC AUC 0.85 for the 2017 state (read from the figure label). Nodes are physical concepts; link when two concepts appear together in a paper.
limits: Single field (quantum physics). The predictor learns where research is heading, not which new link is good. Gu and Krenn (2026) later show predicted-impact pairs do not give more interesting LLM ideas.
agent_relevance: A rarity prior learned from the literature could rank candidate concept pairs before the LLM writes anything. Code-side selection, in line with G5.

source: Wang, Downey, Ji, Hope (2024) SciMON: Scientific inspiration machines optimized for novelty (ACL; arXiv 2305.14259)
finding: Early LLM pipeline that optimises novelty on purpose: retrieve 'inspirations' (semantic, KG, citation), generate an idea, compare to a corpus of prior papers, and rewrite until it is not too similar. Zero-shot GPT-4 gave ideas of low technical depth and novelty.
numbers: Corpus: 67,408 ACL Anthology papers (1952-2022), plus 5,708 PubMed papers. Iteration 1: 88.9% of updated ideas were substantially different; novelty rose in 55.6%; iteration 2 rose in 57.8% of those continued. GPT4-FS+KG judged less incremental in 45% of paired comparisons. Few-shot GPT-4 beat zero-shot in 65% of cases.
limits: Human evaluation was small (six NLP PhD students per Gu and Krenn). Gains came with longer text and added generic terms; ideas were 'superficial recombinations of common concepts'.
agent_relevance: Retrieval-and-compare loop is a code-checked novelty filter. Watch for novelty gained by adding words instead of ideas (length bias, G5).

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? Large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers (arXiv 2409.04109)
finding: Blind expert review: LLM-written ideas were rated more novel than expert-written ideas, with similar scores on feasibility and effectiveness.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition (Human, AI, AI + human rerank). 79 reviewers, 298 reviews. Test 1 (reviews as data): novelty 4.84 (human) vs 5.64 (AI) vs 5.81 (rerank), p<0.01 Bonferroni. Test 2 (ideas as data, N=49): 4.86 vs 5.62 vs 5.78, p<0.05. 104 participants total.
limits: Reviewers judged ideas, not executed work. Standardised topics in NLP only. Novelty is a rating, not a bibliometric score. 17 of 49 rerank ideas also in AI-only set.
agent_relevance: In open mode, an LLM can produce things experts call novel. But see a23 and a24 for why that rating is not enough.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?
finding: LLMs lack diversity: scaling idea generation gives duplicates. And LLM judges are poor at the same task.
numbers: Out of 4,000 generated seed ideas only 200 were non-duplicate (cosine similarity threshold 0.8). Best LLM ranker (Claude-3.5 pairwise) 53.3% accuracy vs human inter-reviewer 56.1%; NeurIPS 2021 consistency 66.0%; ICLR 2024 balanced accuracy 71.9%. Reviewer novelty correlates with overall r=0.725 and not with feasibility (r=-0.073).
limits: Duplicate threshold is an embedding cutoff. Reviewer agreement is low, so the novelty ground truth itself is noisy.
agent_relevance: Supports G4/G5: samples are not independent, judges are weak. Dedupe by code, and do not let the model grade novelty alone.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The ideation-execution gap (arXiv 2506.20803)
finding: When ideas are actually executed, LLM ideas lose their novelty edge. The drop is larger for AI ideas than human ideas in every metric.
numbers: 43 experts, over 100 hours each; 19 human and 24 AI ideas. Novelty ideation: human 4.912, AI 5.778; after execution: human 4.903, AI 4.729. Gaps: human -0.010, AI -1.049 on novelty (FDR p=0.025); excitement -0.052 vs -1.760 (p=0.001); effectiveness 0.078 vs -1.879 (p=0.003); overall -0.628 vs -1.976 (p=0.004).
limits: N is 43 projects. Single domain (NLP prompting topics) with a 3-month cap. Execution evaluation is also an expert rating.
agent_relevance: Judged novelty at proposal time overstates real novelty. A selector that rewards novelty without a feasibility or execution check will drift. Strong support for G3.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The ideation-execution gap
finding: After execution the ranking flips on some metrics: human ideas score higher than AI ideas, though not significantly.
numbers: Execution scores: excitement human 4.482 vs AI 3.896; effectiveness 4.782 vs 4.125; overall 3.968 vs 3.406; novelty 4.903 vs 4.729. FDR p-values for human vs AI execution scores 0.175 to 0.586 (not significant).
limits: Execution-stage differences are not significant on their own; the claim rests on the gap, not the flip.
agent_relevance: Report the gap, not the flip.

source: Gu and Krenn (2026) Generating interesting scientific ideas using knowledge graphs and LLMs: evaluations with 100 research group leaders (arXiv 2405.17044v4)
finding: Feeding the LLM concept pairs chosen by a knowledge graph (random pairs, or pairs predicted to be high-citation) did not raise expert-rated interest above a titles-only GPT baseline.
numbers: More than 100 Max Planck group leaders rated 4,400+ ideas (48 each; 84.3% completion). Mean interest: high-citation-predicted pairs 2.350 (SEM 0.034), random pairs 2.446 (0.035), titles-only baseline 2.414 (0.036). Overall mean 2.40; 24.9% rated 4 or 5. High-citation pairs weakly less interesting than random (reported 1.94 sigma).
limits: Interest, not novelty or validity. Max Planck scientists in many fields. Idea ratings are subjective.
agent_relevance: Selecting by predicted impact or rarity does not buy interest by itself. Citation-style signals and expert taste can point opposite ways.

source: Gu and Krenn (2026) Generating interesting scientific ideas
finding: Interest can be predicted weakly. A supervised network on 25 graph features and a zero-shot GPT ranker both beat chance.
numbers: AUC for 'high interest' (rating 4-5): GPT-4o 67.44%, GPT-3.5 60.39%, supervised network 63.20%. 2,996 ideas used. Citation count of concepts: higher predicted impact but lower interest. Semantic distance evaluator to collaborator: negative correlation with interest.
limits: AUC near 0.6-0.7 means weak signal. Data from one organisation.
agent_relevance: A model-based ranker with a human-labelled set reaches AUC about 0.67. Use as a weak prior only.

source: Radensky et al. (2024) Scideator: human-LLM scientific ideation through facet recombination and novelty evaluation (arXiv 2409.14634)
finding: Facet recombination (purpose, mechanism, evaluation) plus an LLM novelty checker that compares an idea with retrieved papers facet by facet. The checker helped users drop unoriginal ideas, but did not raise confidence overall.
numbers: Annotation: 51 ideas, kappa 0.64 (three classes) then 0.68 (binary); 67 consensus labels (39 novel, 28 not novel). User study: 17 participants did the novelty task; checker used about 6 times per session; confidence change not significant (sign test S=5.00, n.s.).
limits: Very small samples. Held-out test set from 67 labels only. 'Novel' verdicts were less trusted than 'not novel' verdicts, since absence of overlap is harder to verify.
agent_relevance: 'Not novel' is checkable (find the overlap); 'novel' is not. Design novelty gates as overlap searches that can reject, not as certificates.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist (arXiv 2502.18864)
finding: Multi-agent hypothesis generator with tournament ranking by Elo auto-evaluation. Novelty is a stated default criterion and is judged by reflection and literature checks.
numbers: 203 research goals in the Elo scaling study. Expert evaluation on 11 of 15 curated goals: average preference rank 2.36; novelty 3.64 and impact 3.09 out of 5. Elo concordance with GPQA diamond accuracy; top-1 accuracy 78.4%.
limits: Tiny expert sample (11 goals), subjective. Authors state ratings reflect subjective expert assessments, not objective ground truth. Elo is an LLM self-judging loop.
agent_relevance: Self-ranked tournaments improve judged quality, but the judge is a model (G5 warning). Elo was calibrated on GPQA correctness, not on novelty.
